extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, students of literary craft, and readers interested in novel theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes EM Forster's criteria and observations about the novel (character, plot, form) as presented in a blog review of Aspects of the Novel. Useful for writers thinking about novel craft and literary theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round vs. Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: "if a character changes, or is capable of change, it is round. If not, it is flat."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster's strict definition: capacity for change distinguishes round characters from flat ones. Practical implication: aim to create characters capable of development or interior complexity rather than static types. The review notes this is a celebrated and commonly taught distinction (often extracted in course readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs. Plot (sequence vs. causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story focuses on sequence (the 'what next'); plot focuses on causality (the 'why'). Example: "'The king died and then the queen died' is a story. 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief' is a plot."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to decide whether your narration should emphasize chronological events or the causal relationships that give them meaning. Anti-pattern: confusing mere chronological recounting with a causal, meaningful structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel as means to know characters intimately
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster: "in the novel we can know people perfectly, and, apart from the general pleasure of reading, we can find here a compensation for their dimness in life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the novel's capacity to render interiority and human complexity. Aim for depth of character knowledge that compensates for the limits of real-life intimacy; prioritize scenes and techniques that reveal character interiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' autonomy vs. authorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster describes characters as arriving "full of the spirit of mutiny... they try to live their own lives and are consequently often engaged in treason against the main scheme of the book. They 'run away,' they 'get out of hand'... if they are given complete freedom they kick the book to pieces, and if they are kept too sternly in check, they revenge themselves by dying, and destroy it by intestinal decay."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is required: allow characters enough freedom to feel alive and unpredictable, but maintain sufficient authorial shaping so the work holds together. Anti-patterns: (a) total laissez-faire that breaks narrative coherence; (b) over-control that results in lifeless characters (who 'die' or cause decay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot planning vs. organic growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster questions: "After all, why has a novel to be planned? Cannot it grow? ... Cannot the novelist throw himself into it and be carried along to some goal that he does not foresee?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether to outline tightly or allow discovery/organic development. Beware treating plot as an inherited 'fetish' from drama (i.e., imposing stage-like causality unnecessarily). Both planned and emergent approaches are valid; choose the approach that serves the novel's genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing stage-like closure if inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster: "Why need it close, as a play closes? Cannot it open out?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't feel obliged to force a novel into a neat theatrical closure. Consider open-ended or expansive forms when they better reflect the work's aims. Anti-pattern: assuming every novel must resolve like a play because of theatrical precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental structure must achieve coherence, not novelty alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster examines Gide's Les Faux Monnayeurs hoping for an alternative framework but finds it to be only "various bundles of words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimenting with form or nontraditional structures, ensure the experiment produces discernible artistic or thematic payoff rather than incoherence. Novel frameworks should serve deeper aims, not just novelty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical definition versus practical instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Through most of this slim volume, Forster "sticks to definitions. He wants to tell us what a novel is rather than how to write one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you seek practical, step-by-step craft instruction (e.g., how to create rounded characters or transform story into plot), supplement theoretical texts like Forster with craft-focused books (the review recommends Lisa Cron's Wired for Story). Use theoretical insights to inform perspective, but turn to practical manuals for technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism can mislead—prefer reading the work ('follow the bird')
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster's bird/shadow metaphor: criticism can carry readers into regions "which have nothing to do with anything they have read." He advises: "Maybe read a novel instead... Follow the book that is the bird and not the shadow book that is the criticism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let theory or academic criticism substitute for the primary experience of reading novels. When stuck or overwhelmed by competing theories, return to close reading of novels themselves to learn craft and feel what works in practice.
